deck.title: Linear systems through Kirchhoff circuits
deck.visual_contract: Each slide is a single ImageGen-generated raster image embedded full-slide.
deck.delivery_context: 120-minute Week 3 teaching deck; timing appears only in speaker notes and package metadata, never in student-facing slide content.
deck.branding_override: No branding, logo, watermark, URL, footer, or institutional mark is permitted.
deck.canvas: 16:9 pure white canvas; no outer border or frame; no mesh, network, molecular, corner, texture, gradient, or background decoration; locked Roboto Condensed Bold navy title and Roboto Medium charcoal subtitle at the same upper-left anchor on every slide

slides.title: Linear systems through Kirchhoff circuits
slides.subtitle: Week 3 | Equations, matrices, solvability, and physical validation
visual_text: A matrix is useful only after every row has a physical origin.
Can circuit laws turn simultaneous unknowns into a defensible solution?

notes.checkpoint: Ask what must be known before MATLAB can solve for an unknown circuit voltage.
notes.transition: Position matrix solving as one stage in a longer physical argument.

slides.title: Today’s arc: circuit model → evidence
slides.subtitle: The physical law must remain visible after the equations become a matrix.
visual_text: 3 Assemble A x = b with units

notes.checkpoint: Which stage would be skipped if AI returned a matrix immediately from a circuit image?
notes.transition: Connect linear systems to several physical settings before focusing on circuits.

slides.title: Linear systems express simultaneous constraints
slides.subtitle: Several unknowns must satisfy several physical laws at the same time.
visual_text: A x = b is the computational form — not the physical explanation
Every row needs a law; every column needs one declared unknown

notes.checkpoint: Ask students to name the law behind a matrix row in one non-circuit example.
notes.transition: Introduce the two-node network and make predictions before equations.

slides.title: Worked network: two unknown node voltages
slides.subtitle: Known source and resistor values constrain V_A and V_B.

notes.checkpoint: Predict every branch-current direction without calculating magnitudes.
notes.transition: Lock the reference node, unknown vector, and current signs.

slides.title: Declare unknowns, reference, and signs first
slides.subtitle: A sign convention turns a circuit sketch into testable equations.
visual_text: Positive currents: source→A | A→ground | A→B | B→ground
Negative current later means the true direction opposes the declaration
Do not change sign conventions halfway through the derivation

notes.checkpoint: Ask whether a negative solution is automatically unphysical.
notes.transition: Apply KCL to each unknown node before showing any matrix.

slides.title: Derive each Kirchhoff equation before the matrix
slides.subtitle: Current entering equals current leaving at every node.
visual_text: Every term is a current in amperes
Check direction, denominator, and node voltage difference
The equations are the physics; the matrix is their organised form

notes.checkpoint: Have students explain why the R3 current appears in both equations with related signs.
notes.transition: Rearrange coefficients by unknown while preserving units.

slides.title: Assemble the unit-consistent matrix
slides.subtitle: Conductance × voltage = current in every row
visual_text: Off-diagonal −1/R3 terms encode coupling between A and B

notes.checkpoint: Ask students to map each matrix coefficient back to one current term.
notes.transition: Inspect whether the assembled system has a unique and stable-enough solution.

slides.title: Solvability comes before a numerical answer
slides.subtitle: Rank and conditioning answer different questions.
visual_text: Full rank: rank(G) = 2 → one algebraic solution
Singular system: missing or dependent physical constraint
Condition number: possible amplification of relative perturbations
Moderate κ is reassuring — not proof of physical correctness

notes.checkpoint: What circuit-modelling mistake could leave a node floating and make the system singular?
notes.transition: Solve directly and avoid an unnecessary explicit inverse.

slides.title: Solve the linear system in MATLAB
slides.subtitle: Use the backslash operator; avoid an explicit inverse
visual_text: Less work | better numerical practice | clearer intent

notes.checkpoint: Compare the computed voltage ordering with the original prediction.
notes.transition: Translate the two node voltages back into four branch currents.

slides.title: Reconstruct branch currents from the solution
slides.subtitle: A vector of voltages becomes physical evidence through Ohm’s law.
visual_text: All signs agree with the predicted directions
Node B passes exactly the current received from node A to ground

notes.checkpoint: Ask which two currents must match at node B and why.
notes.transition: Separate algebraic residual evidence from physical validation.

slides.title: The residual checks the assembled equations
slides.subtitle: A small residual is necessary evidence — not physical proof.
visual_text: Small residual: the computed v satisfies the supplied matrix
Blind spot: a wrongly assembled matrix can also have a tiny residual
Return to the original conservation laws

notes.checkpoint: Ask for one wrong matrix that MATLAB could solve accurately.
notes.transition: Reconstruct KCL directly from branch currents.

slides.title: Kirchhoff checks reconnect algebra to physics
slides.subtitle: Independent current balances test the reconstructed circuit.
visual_text: Voltage ordering: 12 V > 6.20690 V > 4.13793 V > 0 V
Checks should fail for different reasons
Agreement with a prediction adds interpretable evidence

notes.checkpoint: Ask what a sign error in the R3 term would do to each node balance.
notes.transition: Add a whole-network energy-rate check through power.

slides.title: Power balance tests the whole ideal network
slides.subtitle: Source power supplied should equal resistor power dissipated.
visual_text: Baseline balance: relative mismatch near machine precision
A failed balance suggests a sign, branch-current, or component error
Limitation: the check assumes ideal steady DC components

notes.checkpoint: Why are resistor powers non-negative even when a declared current is negative?
notes.transition: Contrast residual size with sensitivity to changed component values.

slides.title: Conditioning and residual answer different questions
slides.subtitle: A weakly grounded node can be sensitive and still solve with a tiny residual.
visual_text: Residual: did we solve these equations accurately?
Conditioning: could small input changes produce larger output changes?
Model uncertainty: do the resistor values and assumptions represent reality?
Increase R4 from 10 Ω to 1 MΩ → node B becomes weakly grounded
Use controlled perturbations to observe sensitivity

notes.checkpoint: Ask whether condition number can be reported as the actual percentage error.
notes.transition: Show a compact failure catalogue and the check that exposes each defect.

slides.title: Plausible matrices can encode the wrong circuit
slides.subtitle: Diagnose coefficients by tracing them back to physical terms.
visual_text: Wrong off-diagonal sign: coupling current reversed
Wrong right-hand side: source moved or polarity lost
Mixed units: kΩ combined with Ω
Controls: equation derivation | unit map | residual | Kirchhoff balance | power

notes.checkpoint: Give one defective coefficient and ask which independent test would expose it first.
notes.transition: Transfer the same reasoning to mesh currents in the practical.

slides.title: Practical transfer: two-loop mesh currents
slides.subtitle: Derive KVL equations, solve, then defend current and power evidence.
visual_text: Evidence: rank | conditioning | residual | KVL | power

notes.checkpoint: Predict which mesh current is larger before showing the reference values.
notes.transition: Open bounded capstone problem spaces without forcing an early topic choice.

slides.title: Capstone questions begin with validation evidence
slides.subtitle: Choose a bounded physical question before choosing a favourite function.
visual_text: Circuit or sensor network → conservation + residual
Motion or decay → convergence + analytic case
This week: record candidates; final selection comes later

notes.checkpoint: Ask each group for one observable output and one independent check for a candidate space.
notes.transition: Close by reconnecting the matrix solve to the complete computational-physics chain.

slides.title: A defensible matrix solution returns to physics
slides.subtitle: The practical begins with equations and ends with evidence.
visual_text: Model + signs → equations → unit-consistent matrix → rank + conditioning → backslash solve → residual → Kirchhoff + power → interpretation
Remember: a small residual can validate the wrong equations
Practical: two-loop circuit, controlled changes, AI decision record, capstone candidates
Trust comes from independent checks that can fail differently

notes.checkpoint: Exit prompt: name one algebraic check and one physical check, and explain the difference.
notes.transition: Direct students to the Week 03 individual check before group practical work.
